title: A container keeps restarting in production — how do you find the root cause (`docker logs`, exit codes, `OOMKilled`, failing healthcheck, bad entrypoint)?
shortTitle: Scenario — A Container Keeps Restarting in Production: Finding the Root Cause

s1_definition.profdef: A container that keeps restarting is being terminated and relaunched by the runtime or orchestrator because its main process exits or is killed, or because a health probe fails. Diagnosing it means reading the container's logs for application errors, inspecting the exit code to classify why the process ended, checking whether it was OOMKilled (terminated for exceeding its memory limit), checking whether a liveness or readiness probe is failing, and verifying the entrypoint and configuration are correct. In Kubernetes this manifests as CrashLoopBackOff, where the system backs off with increasing delay between restarts.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a new teller at the National Bank of India who keeps walking out of the branch minutes after arriving, and the manager keeps hiring a replacement who also leaves. To find out why, you do not guess; you check the teller's exit note (the logs and exit code): did they collapse from exhaustion because the workload exceeded what they could carry (OOMKilled, out of memory), did the branch inspector keep declaring them unfit at the door so they were sent home (a failing health probe), or did they show up to the wrong address with the wrong key and could never start work at all (a bad entrypoint or missing config)? Each exit note points to a different fix, and the manager spaces out rehiring so the branch is not thrashing (the backoff).
s1_definition.oneliner: A restarting container is a dying or failing process, so read its logs and exit code, check for OOMKilled, check failing health probes, and verify the entrypoint and config to classify and fix the real cause.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A container that keeps restarting is being terminated and relaunched by the runtime or orchestrator because its main process exits or is killed, or because a health probe fails. Diagnosing it means reading the container's logs for application errors, inspecting the exit code to classify why the process ended, checking whether it was OOMKilled (terminated for exceeding its memory limit), checking whether a liveness or readiness probe is failing, and verifying the entrypoint and configuration are correct. In Kubernetes this manifests as CrashLoopBackOff, where the system backs off with increasing delay between restarts.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a new teller at the National Bank of India who keeps walking out of the branch minutes after arriving, and the manager keeps hiring a replacement who also leaves. To find out why, you do not guess; you check the teller's exit note (the logs and exit code): did they collapse from exhaustion because the workload exceeded what they could carry (OOMKilled, out of memory), did the branch inspector keep declaring them unfit at the door so they were sent home (a failing health probe), or did they show up to the wrong address with the wrong key and could never start work at all (a bad entrypoint or missing config)? Each exit note points to a different fix, and the manager spaces out rehiring so the branch is not thrashing (the backoff).

**One line to remember:** A restarting container is a dying or failing process, so read its logs and exit code, check for OOMKilled, check failing health probes, and verify the entrypoint and config to classify and fix the real cause.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the logs, because they usually contain the application's own error. With Docker you run `docker logs <container>`, and crucially `docker logs --previous` or in Kubernetes `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` to see the logs from the crashed instance before it restarted, since the current instance may have no output yet. A stack trace, a "connection refused" to the database, or a "property not set" message often names the cause immediately.

Then inspect the exit code, which classifies how the process ended. `docker inspect <container>` or `kubectl describe pod` shows the last state, exit code, and reason. Common codes: exit code 0 means a clean exit, which for a long-running service is itself a bug because the process should not have ended; a non-zero application exit code points to an error thrown at startup; exit code 137 means the process received SIGKILL, typically because it was OOMKilled; exit code 139 is a segmentation fault; exit code 143 is SIGTERM, a graceful stop. The reason field often says `OOMKilled`, `Error`, or `Completed`.

Check for OOMKilled specifically, because memory is a frequent culprit. If the container exceeds its memory limit, the kernel's OOM killer terminates it and the reason shows `OOMKilled` with exit code 137. The fix is either to raise the memory limit to match the real need or to fix a memory leak or an oversized JVM heap. For Java this is common when the container memory limit is set but the JVM heap is not aligned to it, so the JVM tries to use more than the cgroup allows.

Check the health probes, because a failing liveness probe causes endless restarts even when the app is fine. In Kubernetes a liveness probe that fails makes the kubelet kill and restart the container; if the probe path, port, or timing is wrong, or the app's startup is slower than the probe allows, the container is killed before it is ready and loops forever. The fix is to correct the probe path and port, and to use a startup probe or a longer initial delay for slow-starting apps so the liveness probe does not fire during startup.

Verify the entrypoint and configuration, because a container that can never start will loop immediately. A wrong entrypoint command, a missing required environment variable or secret, an unreadable mounted config, or an unreachable dependency at startup all cause the process to exit right away. The `describe` events and the previous logs usually reveal which. In Kubernetes the increasing delay between restarts is the CrashLoopBackOff backoff, which is a symptom, not the cause.

A senior nuance is to separate liveness from readiness: readiness failing should remove the pod from the load balancer but not restart it, while liveness failing restarts it, so misconfiguring liveness as if it were readiness causes needless restarts. Another nuance is JVM-in-container memory settings: modern JVMs are container-aware and respect cgroup limits, but you should set the heap relative to the limit (for example a max heap percentage) and account for non-heap memory, or you get OOMKilled under load. A third nuance is preserving evidence and avoiding blind restarts: in banking you capture the previous logs and the describe output before the pod is recycled away, and you resist the urge to just bump the memory or restart without understanding the exit code, because that can mask a real leak that will recur at the worst time.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The transfer-service container in production kept restarting, and the on-call engineer did not know whether it was crashing, being killed, or failing a probe. This is exactly the problem a disciplined diagnosis gives. Reading the previous logs and the exit code immediately classifies the cause instead of guessing.

Problem 2 — One restart loop turned out to be OOMKilled, exit code 137, because the JVM heap was larger than the container's memory limit under peak transfer load. This is exactly the problem that checking the OOMKilled reason and aligning JVM heap to the cgroup limit solves.

Problem 3 — Another loop was a liveness probe pointing at the wrong path, so a perfectly healthy service was killed every few seconds. This is exactly the problem that checking the probe configuration solves, plus using a startup probe for slow startup.

Problem 4 — A third loop was a missing database password secret, so the app threw at startup and exited non-zero. This is exactly the problem that reading the previous logs and verifying config solves.

To make this concrete we will write a Java simulation of a restart-diagnosis tool. We will model a `ContainerInstance` that exits with a specific reason and exit code, a `RestartController` that restarts it with backoff and records attempts, and a `Diagnoser` that reads the last logs, exit code, and probe status to classify the root cause (OOMKilled, failing liveness, bad entrypoint or missing config, or clean exit bug). We will run several failing containers, each with a different cause, and show the diagnoser naming the fix. This mirrors the real triage flow.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four container instances, each ending for a different reason, supervised by a restart controller.

Step 1: The OOMKilled container fails. The controller restarts it with increasing backoff, doubling the delay each attempt, which is the CrashLoopBackOff behaviour. After the restarts, the diagnoser reads its previous log showing an OutOfMemoryError and sees exit code 137 with reason OOM_KILLED, so it classifies the cause as OOMKilled and prescribes raising the memory limit or aligning the JVM heap to the cgroup limit.

Step 2: The liveness-failure container fails. The controller restarts it with backoff. The diagnoser reads its log showing the app started on 8080 but the liveness probe hit /healthz and got a 404, and sees exit code 143, a SIGTERM from the kubelet killing it. It classifies the cause as a failing liveness probe and prescribes fixing the probe path or adding a startup probe.

Step 3: The missing-config container fails. The diagnoser reads its log showing an IllegalStateException that the DB_PASSWORD property is not set, and sees exit code 1, an application error at startup. It classifies the cause as a bad entrypoint or missing config and prescribes providing the missing secret.

Step 4: The healthy container does not fail, so the controller performs no restarts and the diagnoser is not invoked; the log simply notes it is healthy. This contrast shows that only failing containers loop and get diagnosed.

Step 5: Across the four, the same three-step method, read previous logs, inspect exit code and reason, then classify and prescribe, correctly identified three different root causes with three different fixes, which is exactly the discipline that avoids blindly bumping memory or restarting.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Container keeps restarting (CrashLoopBackOff)
    │
    ▼ Step 1: kubectl logs --previous  (crashed instance's output)
    │
    ▼ Step 2: kubectl describe → exit code + reason
    │
    ├─ exit 137 / OOMKilled ─────────→ MEMORY: raise limit / align JVM heap
    ├─ exit 143 + liveness 404 ──────→ PROBE: fix path/port, add startup probe
    ├─ exit 1 + "property not set" ──→ CONFIG: provide missing secret/config
    ├─ exit 0 (long-running svc) ────→ ENTRYPOINT: keep process in foreground
    └─ healthy ──────────────────────→ no fault
    │
    ▼ apply the specific fix → redeploy → verify no more restarts
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A container that keeps restarting is a process that is dying or being killed, or a health probe that keeps failing, and in Kubernetes it shows up as CrashLoopBackOff with increasing delays between restarts. I never guess the cause; I follow a fixed order. First I read the logs, and specifically the previous instance's logs with kubectl logs previous or docker logs previous, because the current instance may not have logged anything yet, and the crashed instance's log usually contains the real error such as an OutOfMemoryError, a connection refused, or a missing property.

Second, I inspect the exit code and reason from kubectl describe or docker inspect, because the code classifies the failure. Exit 0 for a long-running service is itself a bug since the process should not have ended. A non-zero application code points to an error at startup. Exit 137 with reason OOMKilled means the kernel killed it for exceeding its memory limit. Exit 143 is a SIGTERM, often the kubelet killing it because a liveness probe failed. Third, I check the probes and resources: a liveness probe with the wrong path, port, or timing will kill a perfectly healthy app in a loop, and kubectl top shows whether memory is hitting the limit.

Each cause has a specific fix. OOMKilled means raising the memory limit or, for Java, aligning the JVM max heap to the cgroup limit and accounting for non-heap memory, or fixing a leak. A failing liveness probe means correcting the probe path and port, or adding a startup probe so a slow startup is not mistaken for a dead process. A non-zero startup exit usually means a missing secret or config or a bad entrypoint, which the previous logs name directly.

On the banking project the transfer service hit all three at different times: an OOMKill under peak load because the JVM heap was larger than the container limit, which we fixed by aligning the heap to the limit; a liveness probe pointing at the wrong path that was killing a healthy service every few seconds; and a missing database password secret that made the app throw at startup. The senior points I always add are to separate liveness from readiness, because a readiness failure should only pull the pod out of the load balancer, not restart it, so misconfiguring liveness as readiness causes needless restarts; to set the JVM heap relative to the container limit because a container-unaware heap setting is the classic OOMKill; and to capture the previous logs and the describe output before the pod is recycled and to resist blindly bumping memory or restarting, because that just masks a real leak that will recur at the worst possible time.
